steps.action: Pose the research gap: how the interaction of the GIA (bedrock uplift) feedback and the melt–elevation feedback shapes the long-term response of the Greenland Ice Sheet.
steps.quote: Here we aim to close this research gap by systematically exploring

steps.action: Take from earlier work the self-amplifying melt–elevation feedback and its instability beyond a critical thickness, which assumes a static bed.
steps.quote: Once a critical thickness is reached, this feedback can lead to a destabilization of the ice sheet and irreversible ice loss

steps.action: Derive the static expectation from Archimedes' principle that GIA compensates about one-third of ice thinning.
steps.quote: From a static point of view a compensation of approximately one-third of ice thickness thinning due to GIA would be expected from Archimedes' principle

steps.action: State the working idea that dynamic interaction lets the GIA feedback dampen and also periodically overcompensate the melt–elevation feedback.
steps.quote: we explore how the dynamic interaction of the feedbacks allows the GIA feedback not only to dampen but also to (periodically) overcompensate

steps.action: Configure PISM (SIA+SSA, pseudo-plastic sliding) coupled to the Lingle–Clark bedrock module, characterize its relaxation-time spectrum versus load wavelength for the tested viscosities and lithosphere thicknesses (Figure A1), and set up the PDD mass balance with a lapse-rate melt–elevation parameterization.
steps.quote: incorporated as a solid-Earth module in PISM

steps.action: Compare the equilibrium initial state against observed velocities and thicknesses and modeled climatic mass balance (Supplement Figs. S1–S3).
steps.quote: The misfits of the initial state compared to observed velocities and thicknesses and to modeled climatic mass balance are shown in the Supplement

steps.action: Design full-factorial 500 kyr step-forcing experiments at 15 km resolution varying warming (1.5–3 K), lapse rate (5–7 K/km) and mantle viscosity (1e19–5e21 Pa s), with ranges justified from the literature (Table 1).
steps.quote: We chose to vary along three main parameters.

steps.action: Run the lapse-rate sweep at ΔT = 2 K and η = 1e21 Pa s and observe incomplete recovery, self-sustained oscillation (about 109 kyr) and permanent loss (Figure 2 (p. 1083)).
steps.quote: A self-sustained oscillation of repeated ice losses and gains is observed

steps.action: Vary mantle viscosity at Γ = 6 K/km to establish that the oscillatory regime persists across viscosities, with amplitude and timescale changing (Figure 2b (p. 1083)).
steps.quote: lead to self-sustained oscillations (ii) in the ice sheet volume independently of the value of the mantle viscosity

steps.action: Describe the spatial ice thickness, bedrock uplift and ablation area at the initial, minimum and recovered states of one oscillating run (Figure 3 (p. 1084)).
steps.quote: During the retreat phase, the mass loss of the ice is initiated from the north of the ice sheet.

steps.action: Map the response over the full-factorial parameter space and classify four regimes (stabilization, incomplete recovery, oscillation, irreversible loss), with an amplitude threshold of 0.5 m s.l.e. for oscillation (Figure 4 (p. 1085)).
steps.quote: we tested the long-term response of the ice-sheet volume to warming in the full-factorial parameter space

steps.action: Estimate oscillation times (79–309 kyr) with a central-volume crossing algorithm, and find no clear parameter dependence.
steps.quote: Instead we here estimate the characteristic duration of the oscillation via a simple algorithm

steps.action: Assess the sensitivity of the oscillation time to the choice of central volume against a weighted average (under 1 %, at most 2.5 %).
steps.quote: the uncertainty arising from choosing the central volume between the minimal and the maximal volumes, rather than a weighted average, is much less

steps.action: Compute the ratio of recovery time to plateau time and find that it rises with ΔT, η and most strongly with Γ (Figure 5 (p. 1086)).
steps.quote: This ratio increases with temperature forcing Δ T , with the mantle viscosity η and most strongly with the lapse rate Γ

steps.action: Map minimal and maximal long-term volumes across the parameter space; the oscillation amplitude is largest at high viscosity (Figure 6 (p. 1087)).
steps.quote: The amplitude of oscillations is highest for high mantle viscosities

steps.action: Project the runs into state space (average topography against accumulation and ablation area) and compare the trajectories with dynamical-systems signatures: fixed points against limit cycles (Figure 7 (p. 1087)).
steps.quote: The trajectories spiral into a closed loop rather than a fixed point, which is characteristic for limit cycles and non-linear oscillators.

steps.action: Relate the oscillation times to glacial-cycle periods and propose an internal Earth-system variability mode of about 100 kyr, plus a destabilization route analogous to AMOC oscillatory instabilities.
steps.quote: reveals a possible mode of internal climatic variability in the Earth system on timescales on the order of 100 kyr

steps.action: Set the oscillations against small oscillations in CISM–ELRA runs (Petrini et al. 2021) and unforced oscillations in Oerlemans (1982) as other models showing the regime.
steps.quote: its appearance indicates that this dynamic regime is unlikely to be an artifact of our particular experimental design

steps.action: For one oscillating parameter set, vary modeling choices one at a time: point-wise isostasy bed model, precipitation scaling, paleo spin-up, no flux correction, 50 and 100 km lithosphere, rain/snow thresholds. Report a combined spin-up plus flux-correction change that shifts the run to incomplete recovery (Figure 8 (p. 1090)).
steps.quote: we perform several robustness checks

steps.action: Keep the four-regime picture and the robustness of the oscillatory regime to single modeling choices, limited to the tested parameter range and to the simple model setup.
steps.quote: we have shown that the oscillating regimes of the Greenland Ice Sheet under constant temperature forcing are robust against many modeling choices

end.claim: Within the tested warming, lapse-rate and mantle-viscosity ranges, the coupled PISM–Lingle–Clark Greenland model shows four regimes: direct stabilization, incomplete recovery, self-sustained oscillations with 74–309 kyr periods, and irreversible loss.

decisive_move.sentence: The full-factorial parameter scan that maps where each regime, and especially the oscillatory regime, occurs is what makes the regime claim exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the feedback framing (§1 ¶11) chose which parameters to vary (lapse rate for melt–elevation, viscosity for GIA), but the periodic-overcompensation idea reads as stated with the results in hand. Claim: the oscillatory regime faced single-choice robustness tests that could have removed it, and one combined change did shift a run to incomplete recovery (§4.3 ¶10). There is no test against observations. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the runs.

imports.item: state-space trajectories, limit cycles and non-linear oscillators used to read the regimes
bifurcation concepts (Hopf and fold bifurcations) for destabilization routes
Archimedes' principle for the static one-third isostatic compensation

novelty_claims.quote: the interaction of the negative bedrock uplift feedback and the melt–elevation feedback, has, to our knowledge, not yet been explicitly and systematically studied
to our knowledge the GIA feedback has not yet been addressed [...] of the Greenland Ice Sheet

limits:
Review: no review file, open discussion or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence. ESD papers have a public discussion (received 10 Dec 2021, discussion started 17 Dec 2021), and the acknowledgements thank two reviewers for comments on the initial version (inference: changes made in review are invisible here). The author contributions say the initial experiments came from a master's project; that earlier stage is not documented.

Robustness scope: all robustness checks use a single parameter set (Γ = 6 K/km, ΔT = 2 K, η = 1e21 Pa s). Regime boundaries were not recomputed under the alternative choices, and combining two changes shifted the regime. The VILMA coupling tests are only asserted, from forthcoming work, not shown. Ice-dynamics parameters were not varied, and the 15 km resolution under-resolves outlet glaciers.

Observational testing: no comparison with observations tests the dynamics. The only premise check is the initial-state misfit, in the Supplement.

Sub-claims and their statuses: oscillation periods are an estimate_with_resolution with no statistical uncertainty (only a few cycles in 500 kyr). The recovery/plateau-ratio trend is a regularity_in_range. The internal-variability mode at about 100 kyr and the AMOC analogy are suggestions, at most best_explanation, untested.

Order of work: the hypothesis of periodic overcompensation is stated in the Introduction but may have been formed after the runs (inference).

Composition: none_fits because the walk is a question-led in-silico parameter exploration with robustness checks. Exploration does not precede the question, no rivals face a crucial test, and conditions are set, not found.

Inconsistencies in the paper: the oscillation-period range is given as 79–250/309 kyr in §3.2.2 ¶2 but 74–309 kyr in §4.2.1 and the Abstract. The text calls the oscillating regime 'regime iii' in §3.2.2 ¶1 but '(ii)' elsewhere.

disagreements.target: Levermann and Winkelmann (2016), melt–elevation instability studied with a static bed
disagreements.support: Adding bedrock deformation through the Lingle–Clark model shows that GIA can dampen and even overcompensate the melt–elevation feedback, producing recovery and oscillation regimes.
disagreements.quote: GIA can mitigate this feedback: due to bedrock deformation, changes in ice thickness do not directly translate to changes in surface elevation.

disagreements.target: Community assumption that the viscous bedrock response is slow (tens to hundreds of millennia)
disagreements.support: The paper cites studies of locally low mantle viscosity and samples η down to 1e19 Pa s, beyond the usual Greenland range.
disagreements.quote: The viscous bedrock response is generally assumed to be slow compared to ice losses, with characteristic response timescales of tens to hundreds of millennia.

disagreements.target: Bassis et al. (2017), ice-volume oscillations in marine ice sheets
disagreements.support: The simulations show that oscillations can also arise in a mostly grounded ice sheet, from melt–elevation and GIA interaction.
disagreements.quote: While oscillations of ice volume have already been discussed in the context of marine ice sheets (Antarctic Ice Sheet, Laurentide Ice Sheet)

disagreements.target: Ganopolski and Calov (2011), glaciation onset and termination driven by insolation, climate and albedo
disagreements.support: Oscillation times of the order of 100 kyr in the model suggest an internal variability mode that could interact with orbital forcing; this is not tested.
disagreements.quote: While the onset and the termination of glaciation are driven by changes in insolation, climate and Earth surface albedo our results offer a new perspective.
